session.question: How can healthcare workers balanc innovation with sustainability when reducing workplace emissions and avoid the wasteful use of medical resources in imaging and other care, while still keepin AI benefits responsible?
session.answer:
Healthcare workers can balance innovation with sustainability by treating AI as a tool for value-based care rather than an end in itself. In imaging and other services, this means critically assessing indications, avoiding low-value or unnecessary examinations, and using evidence-based appropriateness criteria and decision support to ensure that each test or intervention is justified. Such an approach reduces resource use, waste, and emissions while preserving quality and safety. (palm2023sustainabilityandclimate chunk 1, kocak2025radiologyaiand chunk 1)

At the operational level, sustainability can be improved by optimizing workflows, reducing consumables and data-storage burden, and minimizing staff and patient travel through eco-friendly care models such as telemedicine where clinically appropriate. In parallel, departments should adopt energy-efficient models and green computing, integrate renewable energy where feasible, and implement lifecycle-aware management to limit electronic waste. (ueda2024climatechangeand chunk 1, anudjo2023considerationsforenvironmental chunk 1)

Responsible AI use requires balancing diagnostic and workflow gains against environmental, economic, and social harms. This includes eco-design, responsible data management, continuous monitoring of performance and emissions, and governance frameworks that address bias, unequal access, and downstream inequities. Used in this way, AI can support efficiency, lower costs, and improve outcomes without amplifying wasteful resource use or environmental impact. (kocak2025radiologyaiand chunk 1, doo2024environmentalsustainabilityand chunk 1, ueda2024climatechangeand chunk 1)

Education, awareness, and institution-level policy are also necessary to embed these practices into routine care and sustain measurable reductions in emissions and waste. (anudjo2023considerationsforenvironmental chunk 1, ueda2024climatechangeand chunk 1)

contexts.context: This 2024 narrative review argues that sustainable imaging should be judged across four dimensions: value, cost, risk, and environment. It says low-value imaging wastes resources, increases incidentalomas, overdiagnosis, overtreatment, and wait times, and contributes to emissions costing billions annually. A 20% reduction in low-value imaging could avoid about 7.2 million procedures while improving sustainability. The authors recommend multi-component initiatives addressing barriers at all levels of society and healthcare, with coordinated action from government to individual workers. Radiographers, along with radiologists, referrers, and managers, are key in ensuring only sustainable imaging procedures are performed, considering appropriateness, safety, effectiveness, efficiency, and environmental impact.

It also notes common barriers such as lack of leadership, misconceptions about infection risk, and resistance to change, and emphasizes education as a top priority. These principles support balancing innovation with responsible resource use.

session.formatted_answer:
Question: How can healthcare workers balanc innovation with sustainability when reducing workplace emissions and avoid the wasteful use of medical resources in imaging and other care, while still keepin AI benefits responsible?

Healthcare workers can balance innovation with sustainability by treating AI as a tool for value-based care rather than an end in itself. In imaging and other services, this means critically assessing indications, avoiding low-value or unnecessary examinations, and using evidence-based appropriateness criteria and decision support to ensure that each test or intervention is justified. Such an approach reduces resource use, waste, and emissions while preserving quality and safety. (palm2023sustainabilityandclimate chunk 1, kocak2025radiologyaiand chunk 1)

At the operational level, sustainability can be improved by optimizing workflows, reducing consumables and data-storage burden, and minimizing staff and patient travel through eco-friendly care models such as telemedicine where clinically appropriate. In parallel, departments should adopt energy-efficient models and green computing, integrate renewable energy where feasible, and implement lifecycle-aware management to limit electronic waste. (ueda2024climatechangeand chunk 1, anudjo2023considerationsforenvironmental chunk 1)

Responsible AI use requires balancing diagnostic and workflow gains against environmental, economic, and social harms. This includes eco-design, responsible data management, continuous monitoring of performance and emissions, and governance frameworks that address bias, unequal access, and downstream inequities. Used in this way, AI can support efficiency, lower costs, and improve outcomes without amplifying wasteful resource use or environmental impact. (kocak2025radiologyaiand chunk 1, doo2024environmentalsustainabilityand chunk 1, ueda2024climatechangeand chunk 1)

Education, awareness, and institution-level policy are also necessary to embed these practices into routine care and sustain measurable reductions in emissions and waste. (anudjo2023considerationsforenvironmental chunk 1, ueda2024climatechangeand chunk 1)
